title: Challenge: Meet in the Middle

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only meet-in-middle program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Each half has about 2^(n/2) subsets and complementary sums can be matched. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[1,2,3]`, the worked program returns `false`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[7,3,2,9,5,11]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Return true if a subset sums to 15.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Return true if a subset sums to 15. On input `[7,3,2,9,5,11]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Enumerate two half-spaces and combine their summaries instead of exploring the full product directly. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. Most patterns here explore a decision tree; meet-in-the-middle instead enumerates two halves and combines them. Define the partial choice or subset summary that the pattern retains. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(2^(n/2) log 2^(n/2)) time · O(2^(n/2)) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Test no solution, one solution, duplicate inputs, and the order in which candidates are tried if output order is observable. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `true`. Each half has about 2^(n/2) subsets and complementary sums can be matched. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: For target 15 in [7,3,2,9,5,11], one valid split contribution can be matched to its complement in the other half. Include the empty subset sum 0 on both sides so a solution entirely within one half is not lost.
